utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-04-84bis-PT, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I would just like to confirm that the accused are receiving interpretation and can understand the proceedings in a language they know. Mr. Haradinaj? Mr. Balaj? And, Mr. Brahimaj? THE ACCUSED BRAHIMAJ: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Let me start off by introducing myself. My name is Moloto, and I will be the Presiding Judge in this case. Could I ask for the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Your Honour. Paul Rogers appearing on behalf of the Prosecution today, together with Ms. Martin Salgado and also Mr. Aditya Menon. And our Case Manager today is Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Prosecution -- for the Defence, starting with Mr. Haradinaj's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Rodney Dixon appearing for Mr. Haradinaj, assisted today by Bath-Sheba Van den Berg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Chad Mair, Colleen Rohan, and Gregor Guy-Smith on behalf of Idriz Balaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Your Honour. Richard Harvey appearing on behalf of Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Harvey. Now, pursuant to Rule 65 bis (A) of the Rules, the purpose of this Status Conference is, one, to organise exchanges between the parties so as to ensure an expeditious preparation for trial; and review the status of this case and to allow the accused to raise issues, including issues relating to their mental and physical condition. Now I would like to recall the basis for the partial re-trial. On the 19th of July, 2010, the Appeals Chamber, with Judge Robinson dissenting, quashed the Trial Chamber's decisions to acquit Ramush Haradinaj and Idriz Balaj of participation in a JCE to commit crimes at the KLA headquarters and the prison in Jablanica under Counts 24, 26, 28, 30, 32, and 34 of the indictment; to acquit Lahi Brahimaj of participation in a JCE to commit crimes at the KLA headquarters and the prison in Jablanica under Counts 24, 26, 30, and 34 of the indictment; to acquit Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, and Lahi Brahimaj of individual criminal responsibility under Counts 24 and 34 of the indictment; and finally, acquit Lahi Brahimaj of individual criminal responsibility under Count 26 of the indictment. And the Appeals Chamber ordered that the three accused be tried on these counts. Now, my intention is to plan the pre-trial proceedings as far as possible today. And I've seen the transcript of the 65 ter meeting, and I will be referring to the submissions that you made at that meeting. "Pursuant to Rule 65 ter (D)(ii), the Pre-Trial Judge shall establish a work-plan indicating in general terms the obligations that the parties are required to meet pursuant to this Rule and the dates by which these obligations must be fulfilled." I propose to start today by issuing some orders in relation to the completion of various key procedures in the pre-trial phase, and I would like to begin by stressing that the Trial Chamber urges the parties to present any evidence already adduced in the initial trial as expeditiously as possible in the partial re-trial. Now, there are two witnesses referred to in paragraphs 14 and 51 of the appeals judgement. I understand that the Prosecution stated at the 65 ter Conference that it will be able to inform the parties and the Chamber by the 21st of October, 2010, of the position with regard to Shefqet Kabashi and the other witness referred to in paragraphs 14 and 51 of the appeals judgement. Can the Prosecution please confirm this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I note that Mr. Rogers stated also at the 65 ter Conference that a first step is to ascertain from the witnesses whether they are prepared to testify and under what circumstances so that it will be clear what other measures need to be sought. That's very helpful, and I would stress the importance of finding out the position as soon as possible and seeking any necessary orders from the Chamber as soon as possible. In view of the helpful indication from the Prosecution, therefore, I therefore order that the Prosecution file by the 21st of October, 2010, a notification on the status of Shefqet Kabashi and the other witness, in particular on the manner in which their evidence will be adduced and any measures that may need to be taken to secure their participation in the proceedings. Okay. Now, again at the 65 ter Conference, the parties agreed to reduce the length of the indictment so as to correspond to what was at issue in the partial re-trial -- or what is at issue in the partial re-trial with the 28th of October as the dead-line. In view of this agreement or before I even make the order, do the parties confirm that? Do you confirm, Mr. Rogers?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. What we intend to do is to circulate a reduced indictment. My learned friends suggested at the discussion that they would like to see it in advance. Obviously we will get that to them with the hope that we will be able to reach agreement and possibly file a joint motion or, if not, a motion in relation to the reduced indictment by that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the parties are aware of the order that the Chamber issued on the operative indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Dixon, do you confirm for Mr. Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, I do, providing it's in accordance with the order that has already been made by Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Then I'm ordering, then, that the parties file jointly a shortened form of the operative indictment corresponding to what is at issue in the partial re-trial by the 28th of October, 2010. The Prosecution also indicated that by the end of November it would be in a position to present a full list of witnesses and exhibits and the pre-trial brief. I would like you to confirm that, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. That is our current positions. We should be able to deal with that by the 30th of November. But the note of hesitation is, obviously, there are ongoing inquiries. I don't know what the outcome of those ongoing inquiries may be. If we needed to make any form of application, we will make it timely and swiftly, but for the moment I don't anticipate that. So the 30th of November is the date that I'm prepared to commit to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then I would order, then, that the Prosecution file its list of witnesses pursuant to Rule 65 ter (E)(ii) and exhibits pursuant to Rule 65 ter (E)(iii) and its pre-trial brief by the 30th of November, 2010. Let me raise the matter of agreed facts. Since this is a partial re-trial, there is immense scope for saving time by the parties agreeing facts and any such agreements that would contribute to the expeditious conduct of the proceedings. I would therefore urge the parties to seek agreement as far as possible, and I have read the transcript of the 65 ter Conference and I see that the parties are already -- are ready to reach agreements that will expedite the conduct of the partial re-trial. I note that the Prosecution has proposed that a dead-line of the 18th of November for an agreement on facts, adjudicated facts, and agreed issues and that the Haradinaj team proposes a dead-line of six weeks from the Status Conference, which would then be the 4th of November. You will have had opportunities for further discussions since the 65 ter Conference two days ago. I would be very grateful if you could give me an update on where the matter stands. Are the parties coming closer to one another with respect to the dead-line? Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think I can say we are closer, in relation to a dead-line. The 18th of November, the date that I suggested, was to -- for us to try to have put together agreed facts, adjudicated facts, and issues of dispute and disagreement much along the lines of that which is required under 65 ter and would have to be listed in the pre-trial brief anyway. The objective in doing that is to enable us to identify the witnesses that may need to be called for when we file on the 30th of November the witness list. Your Honour, I'm in my learned friends' hands to some extent as to the scope of agreement. We will need to talk to each other. I'm confident there is goodwill between us to try to reach an agreement, and if not, to produce a report by the 18th of November as to where we are. Can I just say this: What I don't think we'll be able to do by the 18th of November is completely isolate, in relation to the witnesses, precise parts of testimony or precise areas of the testimony or statements that have been adduced previously. I think that will be -- that will be too much. But what we may be able to do, and I hope we will be able to do, is identify agreed facts. And I particularly hope we can identify agreed issues. I see a difference between facts and issues, although of course they're related. But if we can reach agreement on broad issues, then the facts will reduce, the witness list will reduce, the exhibit list will reduce; if we cannot, and end up with a lot of detailed facts, then I suspect it will be longer. So as I said in the meeting earlier this week, I do see it as a two-way street. It's not just the Prosecution. It must also come from the Defence, in our view. I hear Mr. Harvey, my learned friend, saying it's the burden on the Prosecution. But pro-active case management in cases of this complexity does require, I think, commitment on all parties. And I'm confident that we have commitment from everybody to achieve that end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before I turn over to the Defence, I just wanted to raise with you a little concern that I see. And maybe it may not be a concern for you, but I want to be sure that it is indeed not. A dead-line of the 18th of November, I'm not quite sure whether it gives you sufficient time to meet the dead-line of the 30th because my -- and, of course, I don't know how you run your case, but it would seem to me that it is only when you know what facts have been agreed and what issues have been agreed that you are able to decide which witnesses you want to call. And if you are going to make that determination only after the 18th, the question is: Will you meet the dead-line of the 30th? If you say you are not -- you couldn't meet it, I would want you to want to come a little forward rather than extend to the 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wouldn't have proposed the timetable that I did if I didn't think we would be able to meet that. I have a view of where the case may end up, and I've taken that into account in the timetable. But as -- I repeat, much of this depends upon how far we can reach agreement between my learned friends and I. What I see is if we aren't able to reach agreement, the list and the document list will be longer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: -- and, of course, the consequence of that is the time estimate will be longer. And the -- that is not in the interests of any of these defendants. So it's in their best interest that the counsel assisting them are able to reach agreement where they can because they know, having tried this case once already, they perfectly know which areas they are capable of agreeing. And they are able to volunteer that to us and that will help us to narrow down the scope of this trial and the witnesses and will help us to get to the issues in the case. So I look to them to some extent. Obviously, I recognise my own obligations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: -- in all of this. But I think we can get there. If we can't, we'll know fairly quickly, and I'll bring this matter back before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dixon -- Mr. Rogers. Let me turn to the Defence. And I'm going to ask you, Mr. Dixon, to comment specifically on two issues - I'm not limiting you to those two - but I would like to hear your response to the Prosecution's submission that the question of drafting agreed facts and issues and adjudicated facts should be a joint effort, not just a prosecutorial burden. And also the next point being the question of the dead-line. You suggested the 4th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I can start by saying, as you'll be aware from our written submission, our request is for a trial date as soon as practicable. And we've indicated certain possibilities there, certainly before the end of this year. I understand that this is not going to be a matter that will be finalised today because there's some steps to come, but it's important to have that end point in mind, we submit, in the particular circumstances of this case. With regard to the two questions, Your Honour, and that end point does then impact upon the answers to these questions. The first, in respect of a joint effort, there can be no doubt that we are a hundred per cent committed to trying to reduce the issues and limit the scope of the trial and the length of the trial. And we are confident, as I said in our written submission, that we can do that within six weeks. We have all heard the body of evidence from the original trial, and it's our submission that much of that, if not all of that evidence, can be admitted by agreement between the parties to go before the Trial Chamber for the partial re-trial. That might not mean that all of it is agreed as agreed facts, but it can be agreed that it can be viewed as a body of evidence. And there's no need to re-invent the wheel, as it were, and call back witnesses if there's no further examination and no cross-examination of those witnesses on our part. And our main point is that the real focus is on the two additional witnesses. That was the basis of the appeal, that was the basis of the order, and that should be the focus of the re-trial. So we are very confident that we can take that body of material and, yes, get agreed facts out of it on the one hand, like issues such as armed conflict, forensic issues, where we don't anticipate that there's going to be any disagreement, background facts, issues as to the structure of the organisations involved, matters like that; and then, in addition to that, have a body of material which can be admitted, we would argue by agreement between the parties subject, of course, to the Trial Chamber's order, without re-calling all of those witnesses to come great distances and with large expense when all of that evidence has been heard already and is on the record. Your Honour, then, with regard to the second question that there that Your Honour poses about the dead-line, we would stick with our original suggestion that six weeks is a long enough period. We have the whole of October to work on this. And in addition to that, we would also submit that the sooner the Prosecution knows what the areas of dispute might be, if there are any on these matters, the sooner they can then get their final list ready. I know the order is for the 30th of November, but we would hope, because it is possible for the parties to co-operate to an extent, where that could even be brought forward, that they could have that list ready earlier. So we could do our pre-trial brief earlier and then be trial-ready for a date to be set. So I would urge Your Honour to go with the earlier date of the end of the first week of November, which is the 4th of November. And if we need time, then the parties can come back to Your Honour and request further time, if that's required. But we don't anticipate that it's an overly-complicated process. It's really looking at evidence that is all there on the record already and narrowing it down. If there's dispute, well, then that material can still be put in as evidence either on transcript or video. And we think we can do it in that time. In the event that we can't, we could always request to come back to Your Honour for an extension. But to start off with, the most optimistic date because we think we can make it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dixon. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Initially, Your Honour, with regard to the issue of a joint effort in terms of agreed facts and adjudicated facts, I trust and hope that we will be able to reach agreement as to most, if not all, of the testimony that has heretofore been presented in this case. It seems to me to be a terrible waste of time and resources for us to rehash that testimony and that evidence that was presented previously on those counts that this re-trial is about. As I look at this re-trial - and I made the point the other day and I'll make the point again - this case is really now about two witnesses, which is Mr. Kabashi and he who shall not be named. And I say that because if the focus is placed there, then there is a manner to rapidly, expeditiously, and fairly deal with the issues that are being presented. And, of course, I think we all appreciate that something being expeditious and something being fair are not necessarily the same, and I'm sure that all of the parties here wish to achieve both of those manners. In terms of the issue of adjudicated facts, I'll take a slightly different view, because as we all know an adjudicated facts is a fact that creates a rebuttal presumption, and it seems to that extent we may be, if we're dealing with this as a joint matter, then we really are in agreement. And if adjudicated facts are going to be presented, what, in effect, we're doing is we're inviting the potential of more testimony and a longer trial. So one would hope that we would be able actually to agree to all of the testimony that has been previously presented and heard with regard to those witnesses that are germane to the specific counts in the indictment that remain for this re-trial, which as I understand it are Counts 24, 26, 28, 30, 32, and 34. If that methodology is used, I think that we would be in a position to rapidly arm the Chamber with not only transcripts but also the videos so that the Chamber is in a position to assess those issues concerning credibility. That would be available by video. And we've been in a position to rapidly, since I know everybody is interested in having this done rapidly, take care of that aspect of the case. With regard to the dates that are being proposed, and as I said before, it matters little to me whether or not it's the 4th or the 18th. In terms of the amount of work that is on my plate right now, I think that you appreciate probably better than anybody what I'm going to be looking forward to doing in the ensuing months no matter what case I'm involved in. So -- and I'll leave my comments there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I associate myself entirely with what Mr. Guy-Smith has just said. The real issue I think that's likely to be taking up some time is figuring out the mechanics whereby Shefqet Kabashi and the other witness can be brought before this Court in one form or another or how else the Prosecution may seek to deal with those witnesses who really are the core issue that the Appellate Chamber has referred back to the re-Trial Chamber. And so it's on that basis that I would say that the earlier we know from the OTP how things stand in their discussions with the jurisdictions where those individuals are, how those individuals are responding, and what the likely mechanics are going to be, then the earlier we know that the earlier -- and I say "we," the earlier you know that, Your Honour, the earlier you are going to be armed with the ability to decide when this trial should go forward. All other issues ought to be capable of resolution between the parties, whether it's on Mr. Dixon's date or Mr. Rogers's date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I perceive a potential point of difference between the Defence as a group on the one hand and the Prosecution on the other, and this seems to relate to the interpretation of how this trial is perceived to unfold. I am hesitant to venture my view on it. I urge the parties -- and I'm sure we all understand exactly where the point of difference is, and I urge the parties to come together and try to agree what in fact they understand is required to be done in the re-trial. Let me just point out quite clearly for purposes of the record the point of difference that I perceive. I hear you, Mr. Dixon, and I saw this also in your written submission, you're pushing very hard for just getting the evidence from the initial trial, putting it there, and then calling Shefqet and the other witness only. I hear Mr. Rogers saying it could be a little wider than that. I could call even witnesses that were not even in the initial trial. But I think it is going to be a big point of interpretation here that the parties would want to agree on as to what actually is expected of us by the Appeals Chamber's directions. And I leave it at that. I have my own view about it, but I don't want to share it. I would like to hear the parties on that. Let me then say that on the question of the date, the dead-line, I will go with the Prosecution for the simple reason that they are the dominus leaders, and they -- as Mr. Rogers said, he wouldn't have given these dead-lines if he wasn't sure that he would meet them. And I must, therefore, accept that he would not be able to meet the dead-line of the 4th of November; therefore, he would prefer to stay with the 18th. However, if agreements are not finalised before the 18th of November, the Prosecution will not know what witnesses or exhibits it will wish to use before the 18th. So the Prosecution would only have 12 days in which to prepare its list of witnesses after the parties file a joint motion on what has been agreed. And identifying witnesses can be time-consuming. And you have told me, Mr. Rogers, that 12 days would be sufficient time for you. However, if it is not, I would suggest that the parties provide an earlier, at least in the first half of November, joint motion on what has been agreed. Is that okay? Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I would agree with that. And it may be sensible to identify a date for that. Can I make another suggestion, and it's this: In light of the representations that I've heard this afternoon, it may be prudent for us to schedule a further -- and it may be already in Your Honour's mind, but to schedule a further Status Conference, in, say, four weeks, in order for us to assess with you progress. And we will then know how we're getting along. I find that often court dates concentrate the mind wonderfully on progression of cases. We'll know how we're getting along and what areas we've reached agreement on and what areas we have not. And to the extent that may be jeopardising the timetable that we have agreed upon today. The reason I say that is that I, first of all, detected the difference that Your Honour detected, but I also detect a difference of approach between my learned friends as to what may be capable of agreement. Mr. Dixon on the one hand appears to be more - I say this with great deference to my learned friends - more pro-active in preaching agreed fact and agreed issue-type determinations; and my other learned friends appear to be more content with agreeing what was said before, for the whole case to be re-tried on paper and/or perhaps with some other evidence. But I don't see it quite the same way. I would like us to try to agree some of the issues in the case, such as the armed conflict, because we made need to take a view on the sufficiency of the evidence relating to the various issues in the case, as it was presented previously. And I wouldn't want us to have to supplement that, if it's not necessary so to do. So my learned friends and I, I think, need to get together soon - I think we will - and see where we're heading. And I might suggestion, Your Honour, if I may, that we fix another date to meet together with Your Honour to update you on the progress so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that contribution. Anyone? Mr. Dixon, would you like to contribute to what Mr. Rogers has just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I would support that suggestion because it would provide an opportunity to assess the dead-lines that have been ordered. And I would also ask that those dead-lines, as I think they always are, are seen as the final dead-line. It doesn't mean that the parties couldn't strive to achieve something earlier than that in order to make progress. There's no reason why we have to work right up to the dead-line if we can go a lot quicker. And the further meeting in four weeks, if that were to be ordered either as a 65 ter meeting or as a Status Conference, could provide an opportunity to assess how quickly we have been able to move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I concur with the notion that we have an interim date. I believe that Mr. Rogers, however, in some senses, misapprehends what my position is. I am not interested in trying -- re-trying the whole case on paper. What I am interested in doing is not re-trying those counts that have already been tried with regard to the evidence that has been presented. There is discrete evidence that has been presented with regard to counts -- those counts that I mentioned before. We've heard viva voce testimony from a number of witnesses, and we've received evidence on those counts. My suggestion - I will make it again and I will continue to make it - is as to that information, those facts which have been tried. There is no reason to re-invent that particular wheel. And I urge all parties to consider taking that body of evidence which exists as a complete and full record of that testimony and that evidence for the consideration of the Chamber. Now, there is further evidence that may be necessary, and I believe that further evidence can be focused on - as I said before - with regard to those two witnesses. Beyond that point, I think that Mr. Rogers is not thinking about some things which have to do with a series of legal issues that may well arise that will indeed expand in large measure these proceedings and the time that these proceedings will take because there are some very fundamental legal issues that potentially can be either addressed or avoided, depending on how we choose to present this case in this re-trial, limited re-trial, at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think the reason that I side with the general approach that Mr. Guy-Smith is urging on the Court is because when counsel are urged to get together and come up with a list of agreed facts or agreed adjudicated facts, experience has shown that that tends to be very convenient for the Court but very time-consuming as between counsel and things can get bogged down in the precise wording of what exactly has been agreed. It may be much simpler, much more straightforward, to say: As to those counts which are being re-tried, this is the body of evidence, these are the transcripts, these are the videos; and beyond that there is really no need to go in relation to the evidence that is already in. There are other issues, and Mr. Rogers instances frequently the question of armed conflict, when did it start, et cetera, which are almost certainly capable of relatively easy resolution. But as we sit here today on the Defence side, we don't know what other issues apart from that are concerning Mr. Rogers. So the sooner he is able to let us know what it is that he would like us to stipulate to, the sooner we will also let the Trial Chamber know what we can go along with. But as I say, when it gets down to the precise wording of stipulated facts, things can bog down and cause us unnecessary grief on all sides. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Ms. Rohan just reminded me of something, and I think it may be of some assistance both to the Chamber's consideration as well as to Mr. Rogers's consideration, since he seems quite focused on the issue of armed conflict. The issue of armed conflict was not appealed. A determination was made by the Appeals Chamber with regard to this issue. It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. It was not appealed and a determination was made by the Appeals Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It was not -- it was recognised in the judgement there was an armed conflict. So with regard to that particular issue, may I suggest, quite gently, that perhaps the principle of law of the case might be something that would be of assistance to our discussion in terms of a number of different ways of trying to figure out how best to focus this partial re-trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. Again, from what I hear, I can see where the Defence comes from and where the Prosecution comes from. I urge the parties to try and strive towards a common understanding of what is expected because I think this is the nub of the problem as I see it. Let me then say that I'll make an order that the parties file a joint statement on what has been agreed by the 18th of November. Okay. The Trial Chamber notes that on the 26th of November, 2007, the parties filed a joint motion on agreed facts concerning the recovery and identification of bodies as well as autopsy results. Some of these agreed facts relate to counts on which the re-trial has been ordered. Now, at the 65 ter Conference, the parties were asked whether they could file a joint motion confirming this agreement for the partial trial. I understand that the Prosecution and the Haradinaj Defence indicated that they could do this and that the Balaj and Brahimaj Defences were more cautious but certainly allowed for the possibility. I would urge, again, the parties to endeavour to reach an agreement on this and also request that they identify those facts that are relevant to the partial re-trial. Just a small part of the bigger part of the agreed facts. Okay. Now, with regard to disclosure. Firstly, I understand that the Defence teams still have the supporting material which accompanied the indictment in the original trial, and I would be grateful if each of the Defence teams would confirm this. Mr. Dixon?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I can confirm this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Indeed we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: As do we.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So then the Rule 66(A)(i) disclosure has been completed. We can record that. Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosure can only be completed once the Prosecution has identified all the witnesses it will be calling. And the time-line for Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosure will be set later. Okay. Let me take this opportunity to remind the Prosecution of its ongoing obligation, pursuant to Rule 68, to disclose to the Defence any material which in the actual knowledge of the Prosecution may suggest innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused or affect the credibility of the Prosecution evidence. Mr. Rogers, just to remind you of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I'm very well aware of it, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I understand that there was a discussion of the timings of the Defence pre-trial briefs at the 65 ter Conference. Since this is a partial re-trial, I do not consider that the Defence will require much time to prepare their pre-trial briefs after the filing of the Prosecution pre-trial brief. Mr. Dixon, do you have anything to say about the filing of the pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the 65 ter Conference we did indicate that we could follow a very abridged timetable to file our pre-trial brief in order to accommodate the earliest possible start date for the trial. And I would just reiterate it again for the record that because of the nature of this partial re-trial, we would be in a position to respond very quickly to the Prosecution pre-trial brief and could do that in a period shorter than even allowed in the Rules in order to ensure that there is no delay at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that, Mr. Dixon. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I took then and I take now a bit of a more cautious position based on a number of factors, some of which the Chamber is aware of in terms of how quickly we can respond. We will endeavour our best to respond as quickly as possible. And if there is a shortened period of time, we will do our best to do that; and if there are difficulties, we will let the Chamber know what those difficulties may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I respectfully share Your Honour's view that there is not much that is likely to need to be added to what was the original pre-trial brief. I think I should be able to keep within any timetable that will be set by a Court. I think the Court is aware that I, together with Ms. Rohan, have another obligation before the Tribunal which is rather paper-heavy and time-consuming; but, nevertheless, we will do everything we can to stay within any dead-line set by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harvey. Let me then make an order that the Defence teams file their pre-trial briefs within 14 days of the dead-line for filing the Prosecution pre-trial brief, in other words by the 14th of December, 2010. Would that be okay? Let me check again with you. That would be fine with you, Mr. Dixon, from what I heard you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. And as I indicated, it could be done sooner, depending on when a trial date was to be set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed. Mr. Guy-Smith, notwithstanding what you told me, I urge you to stay within that time-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that. If you could just remind me of when the Christmas break is going to be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Ah-ha. Okay. Well, I -- we will do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: As will we.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Now, pursuant to Rule 67(B): "The Defence shall notify the Prosecution within a time-period prescribed by the Trial Chamber or the Pre-Trial Judge of their intent to offer a defence of an alibi and any other special defence." I understand, at the 65 ter Conference, that none of the Defence teams anticipate at this stage that they will present an alibi defence or a special defence. I would be grateful again if you could confirm that. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that, Your Honour, at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At this stage, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And so can I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Now, by the end of November, the Prosecution will have filed its 65 ter list of witnesses and exhibits and its pre-trial brief. The nature of the Prosecution case in the partial re-trial will be much clearer at that time. Now, I take on board what you said earlier, Mr. Dixon [sic], that we could have another Status Conference in four weeks' time. And I did hear the Defence endorsing that. Are you -- I'm not quite sure how much you will have accomplished in four weeks. Wouldn't it make better sense to have a next Status Conference after these filings, after the 30th of November? I don't know. I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, personally, on behalf of the Prosecution, I would prefer it was earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Because I think if we have broken down or have reached log-jams, then we can bring them up -- bring them to the Court's attention. And it may be that together we can resolve them in a way that doesn't jeopardise the dead-lines and doesn't mean people are having to make applications to change the timetable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: The last thing I would want is for us to get a week away or get to the 18th of November and really have achieved very little and then we're having to make changes at a late stage in the proceedings. So I think it would be better to try to achieve a meeting before the end of October. And it will keep up the pressure on all of us, which is no bad thing sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Having heard the Defence on this point and having heard that they do endorse this suggestion, can I assume that Mr. Rogers spoke on your behalf in urging that we make an earlier date?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you confirm that, Mr. Guy-Smith; and you too, Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then four weeks from today -- anybody with a quick arithmetic? Today is the 23rd -- can we look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It would be the 14th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of October -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Or, actually, no. I'm sorry, it would be the 21st. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 21st of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which, I understand, is the same day that the Prosecution will be informing us with regard to the status of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Might I ask, if it makes no difference to anybody else, if it could be the following day when there is no sitting in the other matter in which Ms. Rohan and I are engaged. That would be a Friday. I don't know whether that's convenient or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm actually indisposed for that whole week, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it possible to bring it forward to the previous week?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to suggest we put it over to the following week because as my learned friends rightly point out that we will have produced our report, and it may be that a little period of reflection between us will assist for the Status Conference in the following week. So if there are issues to resolve or discussion that we can have about how to move things on, then it would be better to deal with it the following week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers, you have been arguing strenuously for an earlier date. Now you are changing tact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I did say before the end of the month, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What if there are log-jams between now and then that you said might arise?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, I hope we can unstick them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And, Mr. Dixon, the following week?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm content with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I'm sure you would be too, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm in your hands, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, if I could ask for an afternoon in that week, that would be, again, more convenient from my perspective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. Mr. Harvey, I don't know whether I can meet your request at this time. I have no sight of the court schedule for October, so I don't know whether I'm sitting in the morning or in the afternoon in October. But I can give you a date. I don't know whether I can give you a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'll be there whenever you direct me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. The 25th, Monday the 25th?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Is a UN holiday, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it? Come on. Then we must have -- we will have to bring it forward, Ms. Registrar. Is it a UN holiday?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yeah, it is a UN holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, Tuesday, the 26th. Is that okay? And on behalf of Mr. Rogers, I will record his head nodding to say that he agrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The very efficient Registrar has just told me that I'm in the afternoon. Now, I don't know, most of you are also involved in other cases, so we could make a time in the morning to accommodate you, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 26th we can sit in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: The morning won't accommodate me, but I will accommodate you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm with you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. Okay. Mr. Dixon, would that be okay in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. That would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And for you, Mr. Rogers, would -- that would be okay too?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay, fine. I'm going to diarise it right away. Shall we make time? 9.00? 10.00? What time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Okay, I'll break cover. 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 10.00, okay. While we are on that point - I don't know whether I'm jumping the gun here - will it be necessary for the defendants to be present?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, it won't be. And whatever takes place can be communicated back and instructions taken before and afterwards as is usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As long as they understand it is their right to be here should they so wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Balaj does, and we have an indication that would not be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: For Mr. Brahimaj the same. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Okay. We will then hold a Status Conference on the 26th -- I've made the first mistake. I diarised it for the 25th. On the 26th of October at 10.00 in the morning, courtroom to be determined. Okay. On the basis of the filings that will have been made by the 30th of November, I intend to draw up the remainder of the pre-trial work-plan and issue orders scheduling the remaining preparations for the partial re-trial, including the filing of any 92 bis or ter motions, the completion of the disclosure under Rule 66(A)(ii), the Pre-Trial Conference, and the start of the trial. So all those things I think we should leave pending for now until after that Status Conference. Pending motions, are there any motions that the parties plan to file in this phase, pre-trial phase? Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Not at this stage, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not at this stage. But, of course, that may change, and we'll notify the Chamber accordingly as soon as that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And, of course, Mr. Dixon, while you are on your feet, the joint motion on agreed facts is welcome any time, even yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, and we will be trying to do it as fast as that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm in agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: As am I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Now, do you have any questions or issues you wish to bring to my attention regarding the health or treatment of the defendants in the UNDU? Or maybe let me address myself to the defendants themselves. Mr. Haradinaj, do you have anything you would like to bring to my attention regarding your health or how you are treated in the UNDU? THE ACCUSED HARADINAJ: No, Your Honour. It's all okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's all okay. THE ACCUSED HARADINAJ: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm very pleased to hear that. Mr. Balaj. THE ACCUSED BALAJ: [Interpretation] Everything is okay, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Brahimaj. THE ACCUSED BRAHIMAJ: [Interpretation] I have nothing to raise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Brahimaj. Now, are there any other items that the parties which to raise which I may have forgotten or which have occurred to the parties in the interim since the last 65 ter Conference? Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only matter that does cause me some trouble is that there are very, very few Albanian interpreters available to the Defence. I just mention this. It's not a matter for Your Honour to cure; I'm really raising it and throwing it to the booth across just to see if anybody can throw any suggestions in my direction because from time to time the need, of course, arises for me to speak with my client who has done very well at trying to learn as much English as possible, certainly much better than I have in trying to learn any Albanian. The two people that we have relied on in the past are no longer available to us, and the issue of things like the provisional release decision not yet being translated and available to my client in a language that he can really appreciate and understand is an ongoing problem. I know interpretation issues are difficult here, but if anybody can assist us at all in identifying people who may be able to help me out from time to time in my visits with my client at the Detention Unit, I would be most grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for telling us about that, Mr. Harvey. Now, I must confess my complete ignorance on how you work, particularly as the Defence, with respect to the use of interpreters. Do you use the same interpreters that are used by the Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: They're not usually available to us, certainly while we're on trial they're not because, of course, they have their own responsibilities here. It's normally arranged through OLAD. But my last communication with OLAD, the only person they could offer me was somebody who is currently studying in Italy, and it would cost me about a thousand euros out of my own pocket each time I wanted to bring that person here to interpret. So that's obviously not going to work. I will take it up with OLAD again. I don't need to trouble Your Honour with it. I have to say I was largely using this opportunity to speak to these interpreters who are here with us today and see if they may be able to communicate with me afterwards and see if they can give me any help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Then I hope the interpreters in the Albanian booth have heard what Mr. Harvey has had to say. And to the extent possible, if you can meet him halfway it would be appreciated. Thank you so much. There will be no further business. The Court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: adjourned at 3.59 p.m. 22 23 24 25
